title: Overbound
summary: An obstacle-course race I founded and organised, and whose ticketing platform I built: 336 tickets sold for a first edition held on 12 September 2026.

teaser.label: Overbound first edition: video of race day.

context.title: Context
paragraphs: Overbound is an obstacle-course race I created in 2025 and held for the first time on 12 September 2026 at the Île de Loisirs de Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, near Paris. It offered two formats: RANKED, a timed morning race made of loops of about 2 km with an elimination rule, and OPEN, an afternoon format in waves for anyone who wanted to try.
Around the course, the event ran a festival village with food vendors and commercial partners.

problem.title: The problem
paragraphs: Selling an event ticket is a software problem with a deadline attached: registrations must be reliable, payments must reconcile, and participants need clear information up to race day. At the same time, the event itself had to be built from nothing, with a venue, obstacles, safety cover, volunteers and partners.
I was the only developer and the main organiser, so every technical choice had to stay cheap to run and easy to fix under pressure.

role.title: My role
paragraphs: I led the project end to end: concept and brand, the website and ticketing platform, partner outreach and negotiation, obstacle sourcing and construction, safety coordination, volunteer organisation, budget and the event day itself.

platform.title: Ticketing platform
paragraphs: The platform is a Next.js web application. Stripe handles payments, Supabase stores participants and registrations, and Sanity holds the editable event content, so information could change without a redeploy.
Ticketing opened on 1 March 2026 and sold more than 320 tickets across both formats.

items.title: Two formats on one course
items.body: RANKED and OPEN shared the same obstacles but needed different rules, timing and staffing. Running them in separate time slots let one set of infrastructure serve both.

items.title: Free places and discounts
items.body: Free entries and discount codes helped fill the event, but they diluted ticket revenue, and printed flyers could not be attributed to sales.

items.title: Partners as part of the experience
items.body: Partner booths were designed as village activities rather than banners. The value varied: some created real experiences, others arrived under-equipped and returned little.

outcome.title: Outcome
paragraphs: RANKED sold out about four weeks before the event. Participants gave very positive feedback on the obstacles, the atmosphere and the village, and the first edition reached financial break-even.

items.title: Volunteer capacity
items.body: There were fewer volunteers than promised, with notable no-shows, especially in the afternoon. Next time volunteers are confirmed in several stages and every area has a named lead.

items.title: Setup started too late
items.body: Building the course took longer than planned and relied heavily on family and friends. Site setup and race-day staffing should be separate, with delivery milestones and a time buffer.

items.title: Measuring what works
items.body: Flyers, discounts and partner booths were hard to link to sales. Tracking acquisition and partner value from the start would show what is worth repeating.
